Partial = generic reasons or no prioritisation. Incorrect = a risk list without the "it already failed" framing, or 3 or fewer reasons.

title: Customers do the work
prompt: Some of the most successful businesses get customers to do part of the work (IKEA assembly, self-checkout, Wikipedia). Invent 4 new businesses where customers happily do the work and the business still creates value. For each: what work do customers do, why do they enjoy it, and how does the business make money?
reference_solution:
Examples:
1. Pick-your-own urban farm subscription: customers harvest (fun, family activity); revenue = memberships plus produce at a premium.
2. Build-your-own-bike workshop: customers assemble their bike with a mechanic coach (learning, pride: the IKEA effect); revenue = kits + workshop fees.
3. Citizen-science biodiversity app: users photograph species (gamified status); revenue = data licences to research and government.
4. A community restaurant where diners cook one dish per visit with the chef (social experience); revenue = ticket price.
Make the work meaningful (learning, status, play, community), not just cheaper labour.
rubric: Strong = 4 businesses that each specify the work, the genuine reason it's enjoyable, and a viable revenue model. Developing = ideas where customers clearly wouldn't enjoy the work, or missing revenue logic. Weak = fewer than 2.

title: Look and say
prompt:
Find the next term: 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221, ?

Explain the rule and how you discovered it (what did you try first?).
reference_solution:
312211.
Each term DESCRIBES the previous one aloud: "1" = one 1 → 11; "11" = two 1s → 21; "21" = one 2, one 1 → 1211; "1211" = one 1, one 2, two 1s → 111221; "111221" = three 1s, two 2s, one 1 → 312211.
Lesson: if arithmetic gives nothing, the "numbers" may be strings or descriptions. Read them out loud and change the representation.
rubric: Correct = 312211 with the look-and-say rule. Partial = correct rule with a transcription error. Incorrect = numeric pattern guesses. Reward honest reflection on how they got unstuck.

title: Should we run a pilot?
prompt:
Launching a product costs ₹10 lakh. There's a 40% chance it succeeds (profit ₹50 lakh before the launch cost) and 60% it fails (₹0 before the launch cost).
A pilot costing ₹2 lakh would tell you PERFECTLY whether it will succeed.

1. What's the expected value of launching now?
2. What's the expected value of piloting first (launch only if the pilot says success)?
3. What's the most you should pay for the pilot?
reference_solution:
1. EV(launch) = 0.4 × 50 − 10 = 20 − 10 = ₹10 lakh.
2. With the pilot: 40% → launch, net 50 − 10 = 40; 60% → don't launch, 0. EV = 0.4 × 40 − 2 = 16 − 2 = ₹14 lakh.
3. Value of perfect information = 16 − 10 = ₹6 lakh. That's the expected loss avoided (0.6 × 10). Pay up to ₹6 lakh.
Insight: information is valuable when it can CHANGE your decision and the wrong decision is expensive.
rubric: Strong = all three right (10, 14, 6) with the logic that information avoids the 60% × 10 loss. Partial = 1 and 2 right but 3 wrong (e.g. says 4), or a small arithmetic slip. Weak = no decision-tree reasoning.

title: The call-centre metric
prompt:
A call centre starts rewarding agents for keeping "average call duration" under 4 minutes. Three months later, the average is 3.2 minutes, but customer complaints are up 40%.

Explain what happened using Goodhart's law. Propose a better set of measures.
reference_solution:
GOODHART'S LAW: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Agents optimised the number, not the goal (solving problems efficiently): rushing customers, transferring or dropping calls, giving quick but wrong answers → repeat calls and complaints.
Better: a balanced set that is hard to game together:
- first-contact resolution (did the customer call back within 7 days?),
- customer satisfaction after the call,
- call duration as a diagnostic, not a target,
- quality audits of sampled calls.
Also ask: what behaviour does each metric reward, and how could someone game it?
rubric: Correct = explains gaming of a proxy metric with concrete behaviours, then proposes paired/balanced metrics tied to the real goal (resolution, satisfaction). Partial = names Goodhart but offers a single replacement metric that can also be gamed. Incorrect = blames the agents only.

title: SCAMPER the auto-rickshaw
prompt: Apply full SCAMPER to the auto-rickshaw ride (vehicle + experience + business model). Give at least TWO ideas per letter, then combine two of your ideas from different letters into one stronger concept.
reference_solution:
S: CNG → battery swaps; cash → UPI; driver's guesswork → a fixed fare card.
C: auto + delivery (carry parcels between rides); auto + city tourism (driver-guides).
A: adapt metro "ladies' coaches" → women-driven autos for night travel; adapt Uber ratings for neighbourhood auto stands.
M: magnify → 6-seat shared autos on fixed loops; minify → one-seat micro-autos for narrow lanes.
P: advertising on hoods; mobile air-quality sensors that map the city.
E: eliminate bargaining (posted fares); eliminate waiting (stand-level queue display).
R: passengers wait at "auto stops" and autos come to them on a schedule (reverse hailing); drivers own the platform as a cooperative.
Combined: battery-swap (S) + driver cooperative (R) → co-owned electric fleets with transparent fares.
rubric: Strong = 2+ ideas per letter spanning the vehicle, experience and business model, and a combined concept that is stronger than its parts. Developing = mostly vehicle tweaks, or a combination that just restates. Weak = several letters missing.

title: Hats in a line
prompt:
Three people stand in a line facing forward. The back person (P3) sees P2 and P1, P2 sees only P1, and P1 sees no one. Hats are drawn from 3 white and 2 black; everyone knows this.

Asked in order, P3 says "I don't know my colour." Then P2 says "I don't know my colour." What colour is P1's hat, and how does P1 know?
reference_solution:
P1's hat is white.
P3 would know only if both P2 and P1 were black (then P3 must be white). P3 doesn't know → P2 and P1 aren't both black.
P2 now knows "not both black". If P2 saw a black hat on P1, P2 would conclude "I'm white". P2 doesn't know → P1 isn't black.
So P1 is white.
Key move: someone saying "I don't know" is INFORMATION. It rules out the worlds where they would have known.
rubric: Correct = white with both steps (what P3's and P2's ignorance rules out). Partial = white with only one step, or the reasoning skips why P2 would know. Incorrect = black or "can't know".

title: The barber's year
prompt: Estimate the annual revenue of a busy neighbourhood barber shop in an Indian city. Build it bottom-up (chairs, customers, prices, days) and include at least one adjustment for reality (e.g. utilisation, seasonality, services mix).
reference_solution:
3 chairs × ~10 customers per chair per day (out of ~16 possible slots → ~60% utilisation) = 30 customers/day.
Average ticket: haircut ₹200, shave ₹100, some colouring/facials → blended ~₹230.
Days: ~26/month × 12 = 312.
Revenue ≈ 30 × 230 × 312 ≈ ₹21.5 lakh/yr; festival/wedding season spikes, monsoon dips.
Sanity check: ~₹1.8 lakh/month supports 3 barbers' wages plus rent and still leaves a profit. Plausible.
rubric: Strong = clear capacity × utilisation × price × days, at least one realism adjustment, and a sanity check against costs. Partial = a simple multiplication without utilisation or a check. Weak = a bare number. Anything ~₹8-50 lakh with structure is fine.

title: It's natural
prompt:
Advertisement: "Our herbal pills are 100% natural, made from ancient plants. Unlike chemical medicines, they're completely safe for everyone."

Identify the reasoning flaws and the slippery words. What questions would you ask the company?
reference_solution:
APPEAL TO NATURE: "natural" doesn't mean safe (arsenic, hemlock and many poisonous plants are natural) or effective.
EQUIVOCATION/false contrast: "chemical" is used as if it meant "artificial/harmful", but everything, including herbs, is chemicals.
Overclaim: "completely safe for everyone" (no substance is: allergies, pregnancy, interactions with medicines, liver toxicity of some herbs, dosage).
"Ancient" = appeal to tradition.
Questions: Which compounds, at what dose? Which clinical trials (independent, placebo-controlled)? Known side effects and interactions? Quality control (heavy-metal contamination)? Is it regulated as a medicine?
rubric: Correct = appeal to nature, the misleading "chemical" contrast/equivocation and the safety overclaim, plus specific evidence-seeking questions. Partial = two of the three, or vague questions. Incorrect = accepts that natural = safe.

title: Water on the road
prompt:
Every morning, a woman in Delhi pours a glass of water onto the same small patch of road outside her house.

Generate at least 10 different plausible explanations. Then group them into categories and say which you'd check first and how.
reference_solution:
Explanations:
Religious/cultural: offering water to the sun or a deity (arghya); honouring someone who died there; a ritual for good luck.
Practical: keeping dust down; watering a plant growing through a crack; cooling the ground for a pet or a street dog that sleeps there; cleaning a stain; marking her territory against parked vehicles.
Social: a habit she kept from her mother; a signal to a neighbour ("I'm awake"); a protest about a pothole.
Scientific/other: testing drainage; tracking evaporation for a child's science project.
Check: simply observe or ask politely. Look for other clues (direction she faces, time of day, what's on the patch).
The skill: hold several hypotheses at once instead of locking onto the first story.
rubric: Strong = 10+ distinct explanations across several categories (not variations of one), plus a sensible check. Developing = 6-9 or all from one category. Weak = fewer than 5. Show one category they missed.

title: Three houses
prompt:
Three houses stand in a row (1 = left, 3 = right). Amir, Bea and Chen each live in one; the houses are red, green and blue; the pets are a cat, a dog and a fish (one each).
1. The fish owner lives directly to the left of the red house.
2. Amir lives in the blue house.
3. Bea does not live in house 1.
4. The dog lives in house 3.
5. The green house is not house 3.
6. Bea owns the cat.

Who owns the fish, and what colour is their house? Show your deductions.
reference_solution:
Chen owns the fish and lives in the green house (house 1).
Dog in 3 (clue 4), so the fish is in 1 or 2, with red right next to it (clue 1).
Case fish in 2 → red is 3, cat is 1. But Bea owns the cat and can't be in house 1 (clues 3, 6). ✗
So the fish is in 1, red is 2, cat is 2. Green isn't 3 (clue 5) → green 1, blue 3. Amir is blue → house 3, dog. Bea has the cat → house 2, red. Chen → house 1, green, fish.
Method: fix the strongest constraint, branch on the few cases left, kill branches by contradiction.
rubric: Correct = Chen, green, with the elimination of the fish-in-2 case. Partial = correct answer, but one deduction is asserted rather than derived. Incorrect = wrong person or colour.

title: Solar payback
prompt:
A rooftop solar system costs ₹1,20,000 and saves ₹1,500/month on electricity today.

1. Simple payback period?
2. If electricity prices rise 5% per year, roughly when does it pay back?
3. Name two risks that would push payback later, and how you'd stress-test them.
reference_solution:
1. 1,20,000 / 18,000 per year ≈ 6.7 years.
2. Yearly savings with 5% growth: 18,000; 18,900; 19,845; 20,837; 21,879; 22,973 → cumulative 18.0k, 36.9k, 56.7k, 77.6k, 99.5k, 122.4k → payback ≈ 5.9 years.
3. Risks: panel degradation (~0.5-1%/yr), inverter replacement (~₹20-30k around year 8-10), net-metering tariff changes, lower usage, cleaning/maintenance. Stress test: a downside scenario with flat tariffs + degradation + inverter cost (payback ~8+ yrs) next to a base case and an upside case.
Present scenarios, not a single number.
rubric: Strong = 6.7 yrs, ~5.9 yrs from a year-by-year compounding calculation, concrete risks and a scenario approach. Partial = 6.7 right, compounding done loosely, or generic risks. Weak = no numbers.

title: Coffee and long life
prompt:
Headline: "Study of 500,000 people finds coffee drinkers live longer!"

Before changing your habits, what 6 questions would you ask about the study? For each, say how the answer could change your conclusion.
reference_solution:
1. Observational or randomised? Most are observational → confounding.
2. What was controlled for (income, smoking, exercise, health)? Healthier, wealthier people may drink more coffee, and sick people may stop (reverse causation).
3. How big is the effect, in ABSOLUTE terms? A 10% relative risk reduction might mean 1 fewer death per 1,000 over 10 years.
4. Dose-response: does more coffee mean more benefit, or is it U-shaped?
5. Does it replicate in other populations and studies?
6. Who funded it, and was it pre-registered?
7. How was coffee intake measured (one questionnaire at the start)?
A huge sample makes the estimate precise, NOT unbiased.
rubric: Correct = at least 6 relevant questions including design/confounding, absolute effect size and replication, each linked to how the answer changes the conclusion. Partial = good questions without the "how it changes the conclusion" step, or fewer than 5. Incorrect = equates a large sample with proof.

title: Six words
prompt:
Write THREE six-word stories (exactly six words each) about thinking, mistakes or learning. Each should suggest a whole story beyond the words.

Then pick your best and explain what's implied but unsaid.
reference_solution:
Examples:
- "Confident answer. Wrong question. Learned anyway."
- "Erased the proof. Kept the doubt."
- "Grandfather's crossword, finished by his granddaughter."
- "Asked why five times. Quit job."
A strong six-word story implies a before and after (change), uses concrete words, and leaves a gap the reader fills.
Compression forces choices: every word must earn its place.
rubric: Strong = three stories of exactly six words, each implying a narrative (tension or change), with a reflection showing awareness of what's implied. Developing = slogans rather than stories, or wrong word counts. Weak = fewer than 3. Give one rewritten version of their weakest.

title: Waiting for a six
prompt:
With a fair die:
1. What's the probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls?
2. On average, how many rolls does it take to get the first 6?
3. Someone says "4 rolls gives 4 × 1/6 = 67%". What's wrong?
reference_solution:
1. 1 − (5/6)^4 = 1 − 625/1296 ≈ 51.8%.
2. 6 rolls on average (geometric distribution: expected waiting time = 1/p).
3. Adding probabilities double-counts the overlap (rolling 6s on several rolls). With 6 rolls that method would give 100%, which is clearly wrong. Use the complement for "at least one".
rubric: Correct = ~52%, 6, and the double-counting explanation. Partial = two of three, or right numbers without reasons. Incorrect = 67% accepted.

title: Funnel math
prompt:
A funnel: 1,00,000 visits → 5% sign up → 40% of sign-ups activate → 10% of activated users pay.

1. How many paying users?
2. You can raise ONE stage by 1 percentage point. Which gives the most payers?
3. What does this teach about where to focus?
reference_solution:
1. 100,000 × 0.05 × 0.40 × 0.10 = 200.
2. Sign-up 5→6% (+20% relative) → 240.
Activation 40→41% (+2.5%) → 205.
Pay 10→11% (+10%) → 220.
Best: sign-up.
3. In a multiplicative funnel, a fixed POINT gain matters most where the rate is SMALLEST (largest relative change). But compare effort too: a 1-point gain on a 5% rate may be much harder than on a 40% rate.
rubric: Strong = 200; all three scenarios computed; sign-up is best; explains relative vs absolute and mentions effort/feasibility. Partial = right pick without the relative-change insight. Weak = picks the "last stage" by intuition.

title: Follow the incentives
prompt:
Three pieces of advice:
(a) A private hospital surgeon recommends knee surgery for your moderate pain.
(b) A financial adviser who earns commission recommends a high-fee insurance-investment plan.
(c) Your friend who works at a startup urges you to join it.

For each: what incentives might shape the advice, how much should that change your trust, and what would you do to get a more reliable view?
reference_solution:
(a) Surgeons are paid per procedure and trained to see surgical solutions. Not necessarily dishonest, but biased. Get a second opinion from a non-surgeon (physiotherapist/sports-medicine doctor); ask about conservative options and the outcomes WITHOUT surgery; ask what the evidence says for your severity.
(b) The commission is directly tied to the product. Ask for fee disclosure in rupees; compare with low-cost alternatives (term insurance + index fund); prefer fee-only advisers.
(c) Referral bonus? Wanting validation of their own choice? Genuine enthusiasm with limited perspective? Talk to ex-employees, check funding/runway, compare the offer objectively.
Principle: incentives don't make advice wrong. They tell you where to look for independent confirmation.
rubric: Correct = specific incentives for all three, proportionate scepticism (not "everyone lies"), and concrete steps to get independent information. Partial = incentives identified but no verification steps, or cynical blanket dismissal. Incorrect = misses the conflicts of interest.

title: Extreme users
prompt:
Design a backpack for three extreme users: an astronaut on a spacewalk, a toddler, and a 90-year-old.

1. List each one's key needs (at least 3 each).
2. Design features for each.
3. Find ONE feature that would help everyday commuters too.
reference_solution:
Astronaut: one-handed use with gloves, nothing floating away, tethering, temperature → big pull tabs, tethered compartments, magnetic closures.
Toddler: light, can't open dangerous pockets, wants independence, gets lost → tiny size, a parent-only lock, a bright colour + GPS tag, a "pet" design that makes wearing it fun.
90-year-old: weak grip, balance, back pain, forgets items → a rolling-to-wearing hybrid, lever zips, a front chest strap for balance, a "checklist" pocket with item slots.
Universal: big pull-tab zips (easy to use with gloves, while carrying coffee, for arthritis) or item-slot organisation (spot what's missing at a glance).
Designing for extremes surfaces needs that mainstream users have in milder form.
rubric: Strong = real, specific needs for each extreme user, matched features, and a universal feature traceable to an extreme need. Developing = generic features, or a universal feature not linked to the extremes. Weak = one user only.

title: The missing log entry
prompt:
Facts: "If the alarm was triggered, the guard heard it." "If the guard heard it, he wrote a log entry."

Scenario A: There is NO log entry. What can you conclude about the alarm?
Scenario B: There IS a log entry. What can you conclude about the alarm?
Scenario C: The alarm was NOT triggered. What can you conclude about the log?
reference_solution:
Chain: alarm → heard → log.
A: No log → not heard → alarm NOT triggered (modus tollens applied twice). Valid.
B: Log exists → nothing certain. He may have logged something else (affirming the consequent).
C: No alarm → nothing certain about the log (denying the antecedent).
Only conclusions that go backwards through a NEGATED consequent are safe.
rubric: Correct = A: not triggered; B and C: can't tell, with reasons. Partial = A right but one of B/C treated as certain. Incorrect = treats the chain as two-way.

title: What's an active user?
prompt: A meditation app reports "2 million monthly active users". Write THREE different definitions of "active user" that would give very different numbers. For each, say what it would overstate or hide, and recommend one for judging whether the app actually helps people.
reference_solution:
1. Opened the app at least once in 30 days → largest number; counts accidental opens and notification taps.
2. Completed ≥1 meditation session in 30 days → mid-sized; still hides one-off use.
3. Completed ≥4 sessions in 30 days (weekly habit) → smallest; closest to real value, but may undercount people who meditate offline after learning.
For "does it help": use the habit definition (#3), plus retention cohorts and maybe a self-reported wellbeing measure.
Lesson: before comparing numbers, ask HOW the metric is defined. Definitions are design choices, and incentives push towards flattering ones.
rubric: Strong = three definitions that really differ, what each distorts, and a choice justified by the decision it serves. Partial = definitions given without the distortion analysis. Weak = one definition or vague wording.

title: Significant but tiny
prompt:
An A/B test on 10 million users: the new checkout button raised conversion from 3.00% to 3.03% (p < 0.001). The design lead says: "Highly significant, a huge win!"

Evaluate that claim. What should the team actually consider before shipping?
reference_solution:
"Statistically significant" means the difference is unlikely to be ZERO, not that it's large. With 10M users even tiny effects reach p < 0.001.
Effect: +0.03 percentage points = +1% relative. Is that meaningful? Translate into money: e.g. 1M checkouts/month × 1% = +10,000 orders. Might be worth it, or not.
Consider: the confidence interval (could it be ~0?); the cost and risk of shipping (very cheap here); side effects on other metrics (refunds, average order value); novelty effects (will it fade?); multiple testing (how many variants were tried?).
Conclusion: probably ship if it's free and has no downsides, but it's a small win, not a huge one.
rubric: Correct = separates statistical from practical significance, explains the large-N effect, quantifies the absolute/relative effect in business terms, and lists other checks. Partial = makes the distinction but doesn't quantify or check guardrails. Incorrect = agrees it's huge, or dismisses it as worthless with no reasoning.

title: Headlines from 2040
prompt: It's 2040. Write 3 newspaper headlines about EDUCATION that would surprise someone today: one optimistic, one pessimistic, one weird. For each, write the trend that led there. Then invent one product or service that would exist in that world.
reference_solution:
Example:
- Optimistic: "India's AI tutors close the rural-urban learning gap for the first time". Trend: cheap personal AI tutors in local languages + offline devices.
- Pessimistic: "Universities report students can't write without AI; employers ban CVs". Trend: over-reliance on generation tools, skills atrophy.
- Weird: "Schools grade students on their sleep". Trend: neuroscience + wearables turn wellbeing into a measured outcome.
Product: a "thinking gym" credential (like this app): proctored, unassisted reasoning tests that employers trust more than degrees.
Scenario thinking: extrapolate real current trends, push them to their consequences, and include uncomfortable possibilities.
rubric: Strong = three distinct, imaginative but plausible headlines, each tied to a real current trend, plus a concrete product native to that future. Developing = predictable headlines ("more online learning") or trends left unstated. Weak = fewer than 3.

title: Twelve coins
prompt:
12 coins look identical. Exactly one is counterfeit, either HEAVIER or LIGHTER (you don't know which). Using a balance scale only 3 times, find the fake AND say whether it is heavy or light.

Write the strategy for the first weighing and at least the full branch where the first weighing tips.
reference_solution:
There are 24 possibilities (12 coins × heavy/light) and 3 weighings give 27 outcomes, so it's possible, but only with no wasted weighings.
W1: 1234 vs 5678.
- Balance → fake among 9-12. W2: 9,10,11 vs 1,2,3 (known genuine). Balance → 12; W3: 12 vs 1 tells heavy/light. Tips heavy → one of 9-11 is heavy; W3: 9 vs 10 (heavier is fake, balance → 11). Tips light: same, lighter.
- Left heavy → either one of 1-4 is heavy or one of 5-8 is light. W2: 1,2,5 vs 3,6,9.
  - Balance → 4 heavy, 7 light or 8 light. W3: 7 vs 8: lighter is fake; balance → 4 heavy.
  - Left heavy → 1 or 2 heavy, or 6 light. W3: 1 vs 2: heavier is fake; balance → 6 light.
  - Left light → 5 light or 3 heavy. W3: 3 vs 9: heavy → 3; balance → 5 light.
- Left light: mirror image.
Principle: design every weighing so that its three outcomes split the remaining possibilities as evenly as possible, mixing known-good coins in as references.
rubric: Grade the structure, not memorisation. Correct = a valid first weighing (4 vs 4) plus a complete, correct "tips" branch that always finishes in 3 weighings and identifies heavy/light. Partial = right first weighing and correct balance branch, but the tips branch is incomplete or needs a 4th weighing in some case. Incorrect = a strategy that can't distinguish heavy from light, or one that obviously needs more weighings. Reward counting possibilities (24 vs 27).

title: 90% busy, 54 minutes waiting
prompt:
A help desk has 1 agent who can resolve 10 tickets/hour on average. Tickets arrive at 9/hour on average (randomly).

1. The agent is busy 90% of the time. Why might average waits still be long?
2. Using the M/M/1 formula Wq = ρ / (μ − λ) (ρ = λ/μ), compute the average wait.
3. What do you expect if you add a second agent? Explain the intuition even if you skip the exact maths.
reference_solution:
1. Randomness: arrivals bunch up. When work arrives in clumps and capacity is barely above demand, queues build in bursts and drain slowly.
2. ρ = 0.9, μ − λ = 1 → Wq = 0.9 hours ≈ 54 minutes.
3. With 2 agents each server is only ~45% busy; using M/M/2 the average wait falls to ~1.5 minutes. A ~97% reduction from doubling capacity.
Insight: waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. "Fully utilised" systems feel terrible to the people waiting in them.
rubric: Strong = explains variability, computes 54 min, and shows that waits collapse with a 2nd agent (any estimate in single-digit minutes with non-linear reasoning). Partial = formula right but the explanation of why is missing, or expects a merely linear (halved) improvement. Weak = "90% is efficient, so waits are fine".

title: Why the market fell
prompt:
Every evening, news anchors explain why the stock market moved that day: "Markets fell on inflation fears" or "Stocks rose as investors shrugged off inflation fears."

What's the reasoning problem here? How should you treat these explanations, and your own explanations of past events?
reference_solution:
NARRATIVE FALLACY + HINDSIGHT BIAS: after the fact, we fit a tidy story to noisy movements. The same cause ("inflation fears") "explains" both rises and falls, which means it explains nothing. Daily moves are largely noise from millions of independent decisions.
Test of a real explanation: would it have PREDICTED the move beforehand? Can it be wrong?
Your own life: we rewrite memories to make outcomes feel inevitable ("I knew it"). Fix: write predictions down BEFORE events (a decision journal), and judge explanations by their predictive record.
rubric: Correct = names narrative fallacy/hindsight bias, notes that the explanation is unfalsifiable (it explains both directions), proposes predictive tests or prediction logs. Partial = says "it's random" without the falsifiability insight. Incorrect = accepts the narratives.

title: Attribute listing: the pen
prompt: List at least 8 attributes of an ordinary ballpoint pen (physical, functional, emotional, economic). For each attribute, change it and describe the new product. Then pick the most marketable one.
reference_solution:
Attributes → changes:
- Cylindrical → triangular grip pen for kids learning to write.
- Ink is permanent → erasable thermal ink.
- Single colour → a 4-colour or colour-changing pen for note-taking systems.
- Disposable → refillable luxury pen with ink subscription.
- Writes on paper → writes on glass/whiteboards/skin (event wristbands).
- Silent → pen with a click-counter (fidget pen for focus).
- Cheap → a "pen for life" with lifetime warranty.
- Passive tool → a smart pen that digitises notes.
- Plastic → a seed paper pen you plant after use.
Pick by user need + market size, e.g. the plantable pen for corporate gifting.
rubric: Strong = 8+ attributes across categories (not only physical), each with a meaningful change → product, plus a reasoned pick. Developing = mostly physical tweaks (colour, size). Weak = fewer than 5.

title: Statements about statements
prompt:
A list contains exactly these four statements:
1. Exactly one of these statements is false.
2. Exactly two of these statements are false.
3. Exactly three of these statements are false.
4. Exactly four of these statements are false.

Which statements (if any) are true?
reference_solution:
Only statement 3 is true.
The statements contradict each other, so at most one is true.
If none were true, all four would be false, which would make statement 4 true: contradiction. So exactly one is true and three are false, which is exactly what statement 3 says. Consistent.
Method: for self-referential puzzles, look for the FIXED POINT, the assignment that agrees with itself.
rubric: Correct = only 3, with the "at most one true" step and ruling out "none true". Partial = 3 without ruling out other options. Incorrect = 4, none, or several.

title: Build more roads?
prompt: A city keeps widening roads to fix traffic, but congestion returns within a few years. Draw (in words) a causal loop diagram: at least one reinforcing loop and one balancing loop. Then suggest a leverage point.
reference_solution:
Balancing loop (the intended one): congestion ↑ → road building ↑ → capacity ↑ → congestion ↓.
Reinforcing loop (induced demand): capacity ↑ → travel time ↓ → driving becomes more attractive → more car trips and longer commutes, sprawl → congestion ↑ → more pressure for roads.
Another reinforcing loop: more driving → less public transport ridership → lower service frequency → transit worse → more driving.
Leverage: price road use (congestion charging), invest in transit frequency, change land use (mixed-use near transit). These change what makes driving attractive, not just capacity.
Systems lens: when a fix keeps "working then failing", look for the loop that undoes it.
rubric: Strong = correctly labelled loops (with polarity) including induced demand, and a leverage point that targets demand or incentives. Partial = describes induced demand without a loop structure, or a generic fix ("more buses") without loop logic. Weak = no feedback concept.

title: How sure are you?
prompt:
For each question, give a range you are 90% sure contains the true answer (don't look anything up):
1. Length of the Ganga river (km)
2. Year the first iPhone was released
3. Height of Mount Everest (m)
4. Population of Australia (2025)
5. Boiling point of water at the top of Everest (°C)

Then reflect: how wide were your ranges, and what does this exercise reveal?
reference_solution:
Answers: 1. ~2,525 km. 2. 2007. 3. 8,849 m. 4. ~27 million. 5. ~70 °C (roughly 68-72).
If your ranges were well calibrated, about 4.5 of the 5 should contain the answer. Most people get 2-3 → OVERCONFIDENCE: their ranges are too narrow.
Better technique: start from what you know (Everest is about the cruising altitude of planes ≈ 9 km), then widen until you'd be genuinely surprised to be wrong at both ends. Ask "what would make the answer much lower/higher?"
rubric: Grade calibration, not trivia knowledge. Count how many ranges contain the true answer. Correct = 4-5 hits AND a thoughtful reflection on how the ranges were set. Partial = 3 hits, or good hits but no reflection. Incorrect = 0-2 hits with narrow ranges and no recognition of overconfidence (but even then, a sharp reflection can lift it to partial). Mention the true answers in the feedback.

title: Halve the waste, zero budget
prompt:
A college hostel mess throws away about 40% of the food it cooks. Your job: cut that waste in half with ZERO budget (no new equipment, no extra staff).

Generate at least 8 ideas, then pick the 3 you'd run first and explain how you'd measure success.
reference_solution:
Ideas:
1. Students mark meal attendance on a free Google Form by 10 AM → cook to the forecast.
2. Smaller default servings, free second helpings (people take what they'll eat).
3. A visible "waste board": weigh leftovers daily and post the number on a whiteboard.
4. Weekly menu vote: drop the dishes that get thrown away most.
5. Remove trays (studies show people take less without trays).
6. Leftover-of-the-day transformed into next-day snacks (rice → lemon rice).
7. Peer pressure: a hostel-floor competition for the lowest plate waste.
8. Partner with a local NGO/food bank to collect surplus (zero cost, counts as waste diverted).
First 3: attendance forecast, smaller default portions, a weekly weigh-in board. Measure: kg of food wasted per day (weigh the bins) over 2 baseline weeks vs 4 intervention weeks.
rubric: Strong = 8+ genuinely zero-cost ideas across demand, production and behaviour; a prioritised top 3 with a concrete measurement plan (baseline, metric). Developing = ideas that need budget, or no measurement. Weak = fewer than 4.

title: Three boxes
prompt:
Three boxes: one has two gold coins (GG), one two silver (SS), one a gold and a silver (GS). You pick a random box and draw a random coin from it: it's GOLD.

What's the probability that the other coin in the same box is also gold?
reference_solution:
2/3.
Count the COINS, not the boxes. There are three gold coins you could have drawn: two in GG and one in GS. Each is equally likely. In 2 of those 3 cases you're holding a coin from GG, so the other coin is gold.
"It's either GG or GS, so 1/2" treats the boxes as equally likely AFTER the draw. But GG makes a gold draw twice as likely, so seeing gold is evidence for GG.
rubric: Correct = 2/3 with the coin-counting (or Bayes) argument. Partial = 2/3 with weak reasoning. Incorrect = 1/2; feedback must point at the step where they treated GG and GS as equally likely after seeing gold.

title: Dog-walking app
prompt: Estimate the market for a paid dog-walking app in Bengaluru. Give TAM (all potential spend), SAM (what your model can serve) and SOM (what you could realistically capture in 3 years). State assumptions.
reference_solution:
TAM: ~14M people → ~4M households; ~6% own a dog → ~240k dogs. If every owner bought daily walks (~25 walks/month × ₹150 = ₹3,750/month) → ~₹1,080 crore/yr theoretical.
SAM: owners who'd actually pay for walks: higher-income, working, in apartments, in areas you cover → ~15% → ~36k dogs, at ~15 walks/month → ~₹100 crore/yr.
SOM: with competitors and local walkers, 5-10% of SAM in 3 years → ₹5-10 crore/yr.
Key sensitivities: walks per month, price, share willing to pay. Check against local walkers' existing rates.
rubric: Strong = all three levels with explicit, sensible filters at each, a sensitivity mention and a sanity check. Partial = TAM only, or levels with unexplained jumps. Weak = a bare number.

title: The slippery slope
prompt:
"If we let students use calculators in class 8, they'll stop learning arithmetic, then they won't understand algebra, then they'll fail science, and eventually we'll have a generation that can't do any maths."

Evaluate this argument. When IS a slippery-slope argument reasonable?
reference_solution:
Each link is uncertain, and the probability of the whole chain is the PRODUCT. Even at 60% per link, 4 links → 0.6^4 ≈ 13%. The conclusion is far less likely than it sounds.
Also: the links can be broken (teach arithmetic before allowing calculators, require mental-maths assessments) and other countries provide evidence.
A slippery slope is reasonable when there's a MECHANISM making each step likely (precedent, incentives, irreversibility) and evidence for the links. Then the question is whether safeguards can stop the slide.
rubric: Correct = multiplying uncertain links, ways to break the chain, and criteria for when such arguments are valid. Partial = calls it a fallacy without analysing the probabilities, or a blanket dismissal. Incorrect = accepts the chain.

title: Deadline metaphors
prompt: Generate 8 metaphors for a DEADLINE (e.g. "a deadline is a ___"). For each, write one insight it gives about how people experience deadlines. Then use your best metaphor to design a feature for a productivity app.
reference_solution:
Examples:
- A cliff edge → people speed up only when they see the drop (visibility matters).
- A train departure → it leaves without you, but there's another one (some deadlines are flexible).
- A pressure cooker → pressure builds until the whistle (tension, then release).
- A finish line → people sprint at the end (the end-spurt effect).
- A guillotine → fear shuts down thinking (too much stress hurts quality).
- A tide coming in → gradual, inevitable, predictable.
- A party → a shared event that others prepare for too.
- A gardener's season → work in stages; you can't grow a crop in a night.
Feature from "tide": a visual that rises gradually across the week, with mini-deadlines as "waves", so pressure is distributed instead of a final cliff.
Metaphors reveal different mental models; designing from one gives a coherent feature.
rubric: Strong = 8 varied metaphors, each with a distinct insight, and a feature whose design follows logically from the chosen metaphor. Developing = similar metaphors, or insights that are restatements. Weak = fewer than 5.

title: Don't trust five terms
prompt:
Put n points on a circle and draw every chord between them, placing the points so that no three chords meet at one point. Count the regions inside the circle:
n=1: 1, n=2: 2, n=3: 4, n=4: 8, n=5: 16.

How many regions for n = 6? Explain why your first guess might be wrong.
reference_solution:
31, not 32.
Regions = 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4): each chord adds a region, and each crossing point (a set of 4 points) adds one. For n = 6: 1 + 15 + 15 = 31.
Lesson: a pattern that fits the first few cases is a HYPOTHESIS, not a proof. Look for a mechanism that explains why each new term grows, or test one more case by hand.
rubric: Correct = 31 with a mechanism (chords + intersections) or a careful drawing. Partial = suspects that 32 is wrong and checks, but makes a counting error; or says 31 with no explanation. Incorrect = 32 with no scepticism. The main thing to reward is scepticism about the doubling pattern.

title: Dominated options
prompt:
Five suppliers (cost per unit, quality score out of 10):
A ₹10, 6 · B ₹14, 8 · C ₹15, 7 · D ₹20, 9 · E ₹12, 5

1. Which options are dominated (another is both cheaper and better)?
2. Which lie on the Pareto frontier?
3. How do you choose among the frontier options?
reference_solution:
1. C is dominated by B (₹14 < ₹15 and 8 > 7). E is dominated by A (₹10 < ₹12 and 6 > 5).
2. Frontier: A (₹10, 6), B (₹14, 8), D (₹20, 9).
3. Among them it's a trade-off. Look at the marginal cost of quality: A→B costs ₹4 for +2 (₹2 per point), B→D costs ₹6 for +1 (₹6 per point). Choose by what a quality point is worth to you (defect costs, brand). B is often the sweet spot.
First prune dominated options, THEN apply preferences.
rubric: Strong = correctly identifies C and E as dominated, the frontier A/B/D, and a marginal trade-off rule for choosing. Partial = right frontier but chooses without trade-off reasoning. Weak = ranks by one dimension.

title: Ritika the activist
prompt:
Ritika is 31, outspoken and very bright. She studied environmental science and as a student she organised climate protests and campaigned against plastic.

Rank these from most to least probable:
(a) Ritika is a bank employee.
(b) Ritika is a bank employee who is active in the environmental movement.
(c) Ritika works for an NGO.

Then explain the logic of your ranking of (a) vs (b).
reference_solution:
(a) must be ranked at least as high as (b): every "bank employee who is an activist" is also a "bank employee". P(A and B) ≤ P(A). Ranking (b) above (a) is the CONJUNCTION FALLACY: the description feels "representative", so the more detailed story feels more likely.
(c) can reasonably be ranked high given the description (but keep base rates in mind: there are many more bank employees than NGO workers in general).
A reasonable ranking: (c) ≥ (a) > (b), or (a) > (b) with (c) placed by your judgement. The one firm rule is (a) ≥ (b).
rubric: Correct = (a) above or equal to (b) with the subset logic explained; bonus for mentioning base rates for (c). Partial = correct order without the conjunction logic. Incorrect = (b) above (a); feedback must explain representativeness vs probability.

title: How might we... commute?
prompt:
Observation: "Office commuters in big cities arrive at work already stressed."

Write at least 10 "How might we..." questions that open up different solution spaces (vary scope: some narrow, some broad, some weird). Then pick 2 and brainstorm 3 ideas for each.
reference_solution:
HMW examples:
- ...make the commute itself restful? ...make the commute shorter? ...remove the need to commute some days?
- ...make waiting time feel shorter? ...give commuters control over uncertainty (live arrival info)?
- ...turn the commute into "me time"? ...make crowded trains less stressful?
- ...let workplaces absorb commute stress (a 10-minute arrival buffer)?
- ...make the commute social? ...make it a workout?
- Weird: ...make people look forward to being late?
Ideas for "...turn the commute into me time": curated 25-minute podcasts that match your route; a quiet carriage on trains; "commute journaling" prompts.
Good HMWs are neither too narrow (one solution) nor too broad (anything goes).
rubric: Strong = 10+ HMWs varying in scope and angle, including some surprising ones, and 2 selected with 3 ideas each. Developing = HMWs that all point to the same solution, or too narrow/broad. Weak = fewer than 5.

title: Two guards
prompt:
Two doors: one leads to freedom, one to doom. Two guards: one always lies, one always tells the truth, and you don't know which is which. You may ask ONE yes/no or "which door" question to ONE guard.

What do you ask, and how do you act on the answer? Prove it works for both guards.
reference_solution:
Ask either guard: "If I asked the OTHER guard which door leads to freedom, which door would he point to?" Then take the OPPOSITE door.
Ask the truth-teller: he truthfully reports the liar's false answer → points to doom.
Ask the liar: he lies about the truth-teller's true answer → points to doom.
Either way the answer is doom, so go through the other door.
Principle: routing the question through both guards applies exactly one lie, so you know the answer is negated.
Alternative: "If I asked YOU whether the left door leads to freedom, would you say yes?" A double negation gives the truth.
rubric: Correct = a single question that works for both guards, with verification for each case. Partial = the right question, verified for only one guard. Incorrect = asks two questions or a question whose answer depends on which guard you asked.

title: ₹1,000 crore earbuds
prompt: A startup's plan says: "Our ₹500 earbuds will reach ₹1,000 crore revenue in year 3." Sanity-check this claim in at least two independent ways. Is it plausible?
reference_solution:
Units: ₹1,000 crore / ₹500 = 2 crore = 20 million units per year.
Check 1, market share: India's wireless earbud market is roughly 50-60 million units/yr → 33-40% share in year 3, more than established leaders. Implausible for a new entrant.
Check 2, distribution: 20M units ≈ 55,000 per day. That needs mass online + offline reach, huge marketing spend and working capital.
Check 3, pricing: ₹500 is the most crowded, lowest-margin segment.
Verdict: implausible by roughly 5-10×. A more realistic target is ₹100-200 crore if things go well.
Habit: convert big claims into units/day, market share and per-capita numbers.
rubric: Strong = converts to units, compares with market size, adds at least one more independent check, and gives a reasoned verdict with a better estimate. Partial = one check only. Weak = accepts or rejects without numbers.

title: Red-team yourself
prompt:
Pick a belief you hold STRONGLY (about society, health, money, education, anything).

1. State it precisely.
2. Write the strongest case AGAINST it (as a smart opponent would).
3. List what evidence would change your mind, specifically.
4. Rate your confidence before and after (0-100%).
rubric: Correct = a precise belief, a strong steelmanned counter-case, specific falsifying evidence, and an honest confidence update. Partial = a vague belief or weak counter-case. Incorrect = no real counter-argument, or a strawman. Don't grade the belief itself.

title: Invention by subtraction
prompt:
Subtraction technique: remove an ESSENTIAL component from a product or service and find a useful new version that works without it.

Do this for 4 products/services: a restaurant without a menu, a school without exams, a bank without branches (already exists: why does it work?), and one of your choice. Explain who benefits each time.
reference_solution:
- Restaurant without a menu: the chef cooks one daily set meal from what's fresh. Benefits: less waste, lower prices, no decision fatigue (thali places, omakase).
- School without exams: portfolio-based assessment and mastery checks. Benefits: lower anxiety, more projects; risks include standardisation and fairness.
- Bank without branches: digital banks work because most transactions don't need people; savings on property → better rates; serves digital-first customers (but excludes some elderly people).
- Own choice, e.g. a gym without mirrors → focus on how it feels, a body-positive community; or a phone without a camera → for secure workplaces.
SIT principle: removing a "must-have" forces a new value proposition. The constraint becomes a feature.
rubric: Strong = 4 subtractions with workable designs, a clear beneficiary, and honest trade-offs; the own-choice example is original. Developing = removed components that aren't essential, or no trade-offs. Weak = fewer than 3.

title: It matters how you know
prompt:
A family has two children. Compare two situations:

(A) You ask the parent: "Is at least one of your children a boy?" They say yes.
(B) You meet one of their children at random in the park, and it is a boy.

In each case, what's the probability that both children are boys? Why do the answers differ?
reference_solution:
(A) 1/3. Possible families BB, BG, GB, GG are equally likely; "at least one boy" removes GG → BB is 1 of 3.
(B) 1/2. Meeting a random child who is a boy is twice as likely in a BB family as in BG/GB. Weighting by that: BB (2 ways) vs BG (1) + GB (1) → 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalently, the child you didn't meet is just a random child.
Lesson: the same fact ("there's a boy") is different evidence depending on HOW you came to learn it. Always model the process that produced the information.
rubric: Correct = 1/3 and 1/2 with an explanation of why the selection process differs. Partial = both numbers but a weak explanation, or one number right with sound reasoning. Incorrect = the same answer for both without addressing the process.

title: Enrolments down 25%
prompt: A coaching centre's enrolments dropped 25% this year. Structure your analysis end to end: an issue tree, your top hypotheses, the data you'd collect for each, and a first recommendation you'd test within a month.
reference_solution:
Issue: why did enrolments fall 25%, and how do we recover?
Tree: Enrolments = Enquiries × Conversion.
- Enquiries ↓: market shrank (fewer students, exam pattern change), awareness fell (marketing cut, SEO), competition (new online players, a cheaper rival nearby).
- Conversion ↓: price/value (fee hike), results (last year's toppers fewer), experience (faculty left, timings), process (slow follow-up on enquiries).
Hypotheses: (H1) a star teacher left → conversion fell; (H2) an online competitor captured price-sensitive students → enquiries fell in that segment.
Data: enquiry and conversion by month and segment, exit-survey reasons, competitor pricing, faculty changes timeline.
First test: if conversion fell, run fast enquiry follow-up + free demo classes for 4 weeks in one branch vs another branch as control.
Good synthesis: hypotheses first, data to kill them, a small test before a big fix.
rubric: Strong = a MECE tree (enquiries × conversion or similar), specific testable hypotheses, matching data, and a scoped experiment. Partial = good structure but vague data or a big-bang recommendation. Weak = a list of guesses.

title: Review your decision journal
prompt:
Re-read your Day 16 decision journal (it is shown to the coach alongside this answer). Answer:

1. What actually happened so far (or what you now expect)?
2. Which predictions and assumptions held up, and which didn't?
3. Separate DECISION quality from OUTCOME: was it a good decision given what you knew then, regardless of how it turned out?
4. What will you do differently in your next big decision?
rubric: Compare with the Day 16 entry if provided. Correct = an honest comparison of predictions vs reality, a clear separation of decision quality from outcome, and a concrete process lesson. Partial = describes the outcome but judges the decision only by it, or no lesson. Incorrect = no reference to the original entry. If Day 16 is missing, grade the general reflection and note it.

title: Design a thinking habit
prompt: Design a 7-day "thinking habit" programme for your friends that combines at least 3 techniques you've learned in this programme (from any skill). Include: daily 10-minute activities, how you'd keep them motivated, and how they'd know it's working.
reference_solution:
A strong design:
- Combines techniques sensibly: e.g. Day 1 alternate uses (warm-up), Day 2 Fermi estimate, Day 3 spot the bias in a news article, Day 4 SCAMPER a daily object, Day 5 a pre-mortem on a plan, Day 6 reverse brainstorm, Day 7 a decision-journal review.
- Motivation: a group chat with daily prompts, pairs reviewing each other, streaks, a small Sunday prize.
- Evidence it's working: a short before/after test (similar problem on Day 1 and Day 7), calibration scores, self-reported confidence vs accuracy.
It should be specific and doable in 10 minutes, with the mechanism for each activity stated.
rubric: Strong = 3+ techniques correctly used, a coherent daily progression, realistic motivation mechanics, and a measurable way to check it works. Developing = a list of activities without structure or measurement. Weak = vague.

title: Which arguments hold? (revisited)
prompt:
Day 30: you're back where you started. Answer Day 1 again, fresh:

Which of these arguments are logically VALID?
(a) All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Therefore some roses fade quickly.
(b) All poets are dreamers. Maya is a poet. Therefore Maya is a dreamer.
(c) No cats are dogs. Some pets are cats. Therefore some pets are not dogs.

Explain your reasoning as thoroughly as you now can.
reference_solution:
Valid: (b) and (c). (a) commits the undistributed middle: the flowers that fade quickly need not include any roses (counter-example world: roses never fade, tulips do). (b) is a direct subset chain. (c) holds because the cat-pets are definitely not dogs.
A strong answer now: build counter-example worlds, name the structure, and check every argument the same way.
rubric: Same criteria as Day 1, but EXPECT more: counter-examples, structural vocabulary and a systematic check of every argument. Compare explicitly with the Day 1 answer: what's sharper, and what's still missing.

title: Chai in Mumbai (revisited)
prompt:
Day 30: same question as Day 1, fresh eyes.

Estimate how many cups of chai are sold (bought outside the home) in Mumbai on a typical day. Decompose, give every assumption a number, add a range and cross-check it a second way.
reference_solution:
≈ 20M people × ~30% buying × ~1.5 cups ≈ 9M cups/day (range 5-15M). Supply-side cross-check: 30-50k stalls/canteens × 200-300 cups ≈ 6-15M.
By now expect: explicit ranges per assumption, sensitivity (which factor matters most), and two independent routes reconciled.
rubric: As Day 1, with a higher bar: decomposition, explicit numbers, a range, a cross-check, and a note on the most uncertain factor. Compare with the Day 1 answer: which habits are new?

title: Name the flaw (revisited)
prompt:
Day 30: back to Day 1. Identify the main flaw in each, and go deeper than last time: what question would expose it in a live discussion?

(a) "Don't listen to Priya on the sugar tax. She's always on some diet."
(b) "Either we ban all cars from the city centre or we accept that pollution will kill us."
(c) "My opponent wants to reduce the defence budget. Clearly he wants to leave the country defenceless."
reference_solution:
(a) Ad hominem → "Setting Priya aside, what's wrong with her ARGUMENT?"
(b) False dilemma → "What options sit between a full ban and doing nothing?"
(c) Straw man → "Is 'reduce' the same as 'eliminate'? By how much, and on what?"
Expect sharper naming, explanations that would convince someone who made the argument, and practical countering questions.
rubric: Same as Day 1, plus the expectation of good countering questions. Compare with the Day 1 answer and note specifically what improved.

title: One bottle, many lives (revisited)
prompt:
Day 30: same 5-minute challenge as Day 1. List as many uses as you can for an EMPTY 1-litre plastic bottle. Aim to beat your Day 1 count AND originality.

Mark your 3 most original ideas with * and say which techniques you used to get past the obvious (SCAMPER, random entry, extreme users...).
reference_solution: Same reference as Day 1 (container → drip irrigation, bottle light, raft float, eco-brick, instrument, mould...). By Day 30, expect deliberate technique use: changing state/scale/user, SCAMPER letters, random words, extreme users. That should produce more ideas, and more distant ones.
rubric: As Day 1, but compare directly with the Day 1 submission: count, originality and technique use. Strong requires clear improvement or deliberate technique use. Never "incorrect".
